Marathon Petroleum dropped 3.3% today after climbing sharply over the prior three trading days. The decline follows news that Russian crude production has rebounded significantly—the IEA reported output at 8.73 million barrels per day in October—which is pushing global oil markets back into surplus (more supply than demand). When global oil supply exceeds demand, refinery margins typically compress, meaning refiners earn less profit on each barrel processed.

The broader headwind is straightforward: even though U.S. refineries are running at 95.2% capacity and heating oil prices remain elevated year-over-year, the market's shift from supply tightness to surplus reduces the economic advantage that fueled the stock's 6% gain earlier this week. Supply normalization, particularly from Russia, removes pricing power that benefited refiners when crude was scarcer.
